meta.title: Who really said "What people say, what people do, and what they say they do are entirely different things"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Margaret Mead everywhere — yet Harvard librarians could not find a citation, and the sentence turns up in no work of hers in full-text search. The print trail starts in 1999.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What people say, what people do, and what they say they do are entirely different things'?
meta.ogDescription: Everyone credits Margaret Mead, but Harvard librarians could not find a citation and the line turns up in no work of hers in full-text search. The print trail starts in 1999.

answer.label: Not traceable to Margaret Mead
answer.sourceLine: The line is credited to Mead almost everywhere it appears, but no one has produced a source. Harvard Library’s reference desk searched and concluded, plainly, that though widely attributed to Mead, no citation can be found ↗ — and the only note Wikiquote ↗ offers is that it was “attributed in” a book published in 2000, more than two decades after her death in 1978. The thought is genuinely Mead-shaped; the sentence is not documented as hers.

source.excerpt: What people say, what people do, and what they say they do are entirely different things.
trail: Harvard Library’s reference service answered a direct request for a citation with the finding that though widely attributed to Mead, no citation can be found ↗, and pointed to a scholarly note describing the adage as a simplification of Mead’s extensive writing on anthropological fieldwork.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the sentence with a single note — that it was “attributed in” Teaching Music Through Performance In Band, Vol. 3 (2000), p. 13. That is a book published in 2000, more than two decades after Mead’s death in 1978, and it credits her without giving a source of its own.

A full-text search inside the Internet Archive’s scanned books ↗ turns up the line only in leadership, sales, management and inspirational titles — the oldest located being Maxwell’s 1999 leadership book. Marilyn L. Grady’s 20 Biggest Mistakes Principals Make and How to Avoid Them even footnotes the quotation to “(Maxwell, 1999, p. 51),” tracing it to another business book rather than to Mead.

Quote Investigator’s Margaret Mead file ↗ covers three famous Mead attributions — the healed femur, “never doubt that a small group…” and “absolutely unique” — but not this one. No specialist has ruled on it in either direction, so this page reports the absence of evidence rather than a verdict.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to show — no speech transcript, article, book page or letter containing this sentence has been located. It circulates as a free-floating maxim, in two competing wordings.

source.rightsNote: Because the wording cannot be tied to any identified work, speech or letter, no copyright status can responsibly be asserted — a public-domain claim would require a specific pre-1931 publication, and none exists here. The only printings that can be dated are modern books from 1999 onward, which are themselves in copyright to their own authors and publishers.

author.name: Margaret Mead
author.heading: Who Margaret Mead actually was
author.metaLine: 1901–1978 · American cultural anthropologist, author & museum curator
author.bio: Margaret Mead (16 December 1901 – 15 November 1978) was an American cultural anthropologist, author and speaker who became one of the most recognisable public intellectuals of the twentieth century. Her fieldwork in Samoa and New Guinea produced Coming of Age in Samoa (1928), Growing Up in New Guinea (1930) and Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935), and she served as curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History from 1946 to 1969. That combination — genuine scholarly authority plus household-name fame — is exactly what makes her one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for quotations she never wrote.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. Earliest printing found in this research: John C. Compare “Margaret Mead,” Wikiquote, which records only: “Attributed in Teaching Music Through Performance In Band, Vol. 3 (2000), edited by Richard B. Miles, Larry Blocher, Eugene Corporon, p. 13.”

misattribution.heading: How a research maxim became a Mead quotation
misattribution.intro: This is the most-quoted sentence in user research, and one of the least-sourced. The credit to Mead is universal, late, and so far unsupported by any document.

items.why: Harvard Library’s reference service searched for a citation and reported that though widely attributed to Mead, they could not find one ↗. Wikiquote ↗ carries the line with only the note that it was “attributed in” Teaching Music Through Performance In Band, Vol. 3 (2000), p. 13 — a secondary credit in a book published more than two decades after Mead’s death in 1978, not a source.

A full-text search of the Internet Archive’s scanned books ↗ returns the sentence only in leadership manuals, sales books, supervisor handbooks and devotionals — the oldest located being John C. Maxwell’s The 21 Indispensable Qualities of a Leader, first published in 1999 ↗. One later education title even cites the line to “(Maxwell, 1999, p. 51)” rather than to anything by Mead.

It circulates as both “what they say they do” and “what people say they do,” with both forms turning up across the same scanned-book corpus ↗. A quotation copied from a fixed printed paragraph tends to hold its shape; a saying passed hand to hand does not.

misattribution.truthLine: The observation is real and is genuinely close to Mead’s method — the note Harvard cites calls the adage “a simplification of extensive writing by Mead on the fieldwork of anthropologists” ↗. But a simplification of someone’s work is not a quotation from it, and no document has ever put these words in her mouth.

context.heading: Why this one refuses to die
lead: It is the founding scripture of user research. Every ethnographer, UX designer, market researcher and product manager has heard it, usually in the first week of the job, usually with Mead’s name attached like a warranty. The claim it makes — that self-report is a poor proxy for behaviour — is true, useful, and genuinely central to the observational method Mead helped popularise.

That is precisely why nobody checks. A line that sounds like something an anthropologist would say, credited to the most famous anthropologist most people can name, sails through unchallenged. But the paper trail runs the wrong way: the sentence surfaces in business books at the end of the 1990s and spreads from there, rather than descending from any lecture, paper or book of Mead’s.
detailsBody: Searching the Internet Archive’s scanned book corpus for the phrase returns a tight, telling cluster: leadership manuals, sales and network-marketing books, supervisor handbooks, trend-forecasting guides and devotionals. Nearly every one of them prints the line beside Mead’s name and no page number. One education title, Marilyn L. Grady’s 20 Biggest Mistakes Principals Make and How to Avoid Them, does give a citation — but it cites “(Maxwell, 1999, p. 51),” pointing at another quote-repeating business book rather than at Mead.

The wording itself is unstable, which is the usual fingerprint of a saying that travelled by mouth and by handout rather than off a printed page. Two versions circulate — “what they say they do” predominates, but “what people say they do” runs alongside it in the same scanned-book corpus. A sentence lifted from a specific published paragraph tends not to drift like that.

None of this proves Mead never said it — she lectured constantly, and an unrecorded remark leaves no trace. It does mean that after decades of circulation, including a formal search by Harvard reference librarians, the quotation still has no anchor. Until one turns up, the honest label is “credited to” rather than “said by.”
context.pull: The insight is real anthropology. The sentence is not documented anthropology.
